subject: Biotechnology
title: Rare Disease Diagnosis
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Rare Disease Diagnosis.

hook.text: Rare disease patients wait an average of 5 years for diagnosis — genomic sequencing cuts that to weeks.

buildup.text: There are over 7,000 rare diseases — 80% are genetic, affecting 400 million people worldwide combined.

discovery.text: Trio sequencing analyzes the patient plus both parents — finding de novo mutations that parents do not carry.

twist.text: Only 50% of rare disease patients get a diagnosis even with genome sequencing — many disease genes remain unknown.

climax.text: Matchmaker Exchange connects unsolved cases worldwide — finding other patients with the same rare mutation and phenotype.

punchline.text: Sequence the family, find the mutation — genomics ends diagnostic odysseys.

quiz.question: Why does trio sequencing improve rare disease diagnosis?
options: It sequences the genome three times for better accuracy
Comparing patient DNA to both parents reveals de novo mutations that only the patient carries
It tests three different genes simultaneously

details.summary: Genomic sequencing has transformed rare disease diagnosis, ending diagnostic odysseys that previously lasted years. Whole exome and whole genome sequencing identifies causative variants in about 30 to 50 percent of undiagnosed rare disease patients, connecting them with treatments and support.
details.whyItMatters: An estimated 300 million people worldwide have rare diseases with average diagnostic delays of 5 to 7 years. Genomic sequencing provides definitive diagnoses that end uncertainty, enable targeted treatment when available, and inform family planning
takeaways: Whole genome sequencing diagnoses 30 to 50 percent of previously undiagnosed cases
Diagnostic odysseys averaging 5 to 7 years can be resolved in weeks with sequencing
Diagnosis connects families with condition-specific treatments and support communities

faq.question: Why is rare disease diagnosis so difficult without genomic sequencing?
faq.answer: Over 7,000 rare diseases exist, most with overlapping symptoms. Most physicians rarely encounter any given rare disease. Patients see an average of 7 specialists over 5 years before diagnosis. Genomic sequencing systematically searches all genes simultaneously rather than testing one at a time.

faq.question: What happens for the 50 to 70 percent of patients who are not diagnosed by sequencing?
faq.answer: Undiagnosed patients may have variants in novel disease genes not yet linked to disease, non-coding regulatory variants, structural variants difficult to detect, or non-genetic conditions. Reanalysis as knowledge grows diagnoses an additional 10 to 15 percent of initially negative cases.
